title: Good for the hive
hook: what isn't good for the hive isn't good for the bee (Meditations 6.54)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Caesared: Marcus warned himself not to let the role dye him through. Stay simple.

A shared kitchen: an apartment, an office, a dorm. One person leaves their dishes in the sink because it's quicker, just this once. Then another does. By Friday nobody can make a sandwich, including the person who started it. What was good for one of them turned out bad for all of them, and then bad for each of them. Marcus wrote a one-line entry about this, and it's about bees.
screen: `DISHES IN THE SHARED SINK.` → `BAD FOR ALL, THEN FOR EACH.` → `GOOD FOR THE HIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole entry, Book Six, section fifty-four, in George Long's translation: "That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee." One line. Marcus's Greek word can mean the swarm or the hive: the whole buzzing community. No single bee makes the honey. What we call a bee is really a hive that happens to fly around in small pieces. The Stoics believed people were like that. We're made to work together, Marcus says early in the book, the way hands and feet and eyelids are. So he couldn't picture a good that was only his. If a choice helped Marcus and hurt Rome, it wasn't really good for Marcus either. In Book Five he flips it around: what doesn't harm the city doesn't harm the citizen. So if something annoys you but hurts no one, maybe it isn't really harm. The line cuts two ways. It's a check on selfishness: before the shortcut, ask what it does to the hive. And it's a comfort: you're not a lone bee trying to make honey by yourself. You belong to something bigger, a household, a street, a team, the whole human family, and your good is tied up with theirs. Of course, Marcus isn't saying the hive is always right, or that one person should be sacrificed for the group. He's saying a real good can't be yours alone. Your line: the hive.
screen: `NOT GOOD FOR THE SWARM.` · `A HIVE THAT FLIES IN SMALL PIECES.` · `NO HARM TO THE CITY, NONE TO YOU.` · then, large: `THE HIVE.`

segments.voice: Picture your hive: the people you live with, or near, or work beside, one by one. Then think of one small thing that would make the shared space better, emptying the dishwasher, taking out the trash, a kind note on the fridge, a call to a parent, and hold it in mind as a gift to the hive.
Swarm. Marcus's word for the whole hive: what isn't good for the swarm isn't good for the bee either. Today's word.
Your line: the hive. No bee makes honey on its own. Day two hundred one, done.

howItsDone: The Stoics taught that human beings are made for community, and many readers of Marcus use this line as a quick test for their choices: is this good for the people around me?
